scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance originated in the Veraval and Chorwad regions of Saurashtra, Gujarat.
It was developed by laborers from the Koli and Halpati communities.
The practice began as a way to pass the time and maintain rhythm while pressing lime into house foundations or leveling ground with heavy wooden tools.
on_screen: Map: India · South Asia
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally a labor-saving rhythmic exercise to avoid monotony, it is now performed for cultural celebration.
It signifies the strength and communal effort of women laborers in the Saurashtra region.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Women hold 175-centimeter wooden poles and stand in two opposite rows.
They strike the floor with the weighted end of the pole in synchronization with folk songs.
The movement involves lifting the heavy mallet and bringing it down firmly to create a percussive beat against the ground.
Watch for Tippani Strike.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is driven by the turi and thali (brass plate).
Other instruments include the zanz, manjira, tabla, dhol, and shehnai.
Listen for the Turi, Thali, Zanz, Manjira.

The sound is dominated by the heavy, dull thud of wooden blocks hitting the earth, layered with the sharp metallic ring of the thali and manjira. The turi and dhol provide a deep rhythmic base, while the shehnai adds a melodic overlay to the dancers' voices.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Specific individual performers are not named in the sources; the dance is identified with the Koli and Halpati laboring communities.
The dance is specific to the Saurashtra region, particularly the coastal towns of Veraval and Chorwad.
Tippani is a subclass of Indian folk dance and is closely tied to the occupational traditions of the Koli community.
